Caesar in Gaul, 52 BC: Vercingetorix's rising, from Cenabum to Gergovia: 52 BC: Napoleon III describes the Gaulish town of Avaricum as enclosing 40,000 souls. [Napoleon III] 52 BC: Cassius Dio writes that the Romans plundered the whole city and, in anger at the siege and their hardships, slew all the people. [Cassius Dio] 52 BC: Vercingetorix tells his soldiers that the Romans did not conquer by valour nor in the field, but by a kind of art and skill in assault with which the Gauls themselves were unacquainted. [Caesar]

Caesar in Gaul, 52 BC: Vercingetorix's rising, from Cenabum to Gergovia: 52 BC: Caesar writes that Vercingetorix's dignity increased daily although a loss was sustained, and that on this occasion, for the first time, the Gauls began to fortify their camps. [Caesar] 52 BC: Caesar writes that Vercingetorix took care that those who fled to him on the storming of Avaricum should be provided with arms and clothes. [Caesar] 52 BC: Caesar, after delaying several days at Avaricum and finding there the greatest plenty of corn and other provisions, refreshed his army after their fatigue and privation. [Caesar]

Caesar in Gaul, 52 BC: Vercingetorix's rising, from Cenabum to Gergovia: 52 BC: Caesar writes that, whereas a single magistrate had usually been appointed in ancient times and held the power of king for a single year, two persons, Convictolitanis and Cotus, now exercised this office, each asserting that he was appointed according to their laws, and that the whole state was up in arms. [Caesar] 52 BC: At Decetia Caesar compels Cotus to resign his office and orders Convictolitanis, who had been elected by the priests, to hold the supreme authority of the Aedui. [Caesar]

Caesar in Gaul, 52 BC: Vercingetorix's rising, from Cenabum to Gergovia: 52 BC: Caesar asks the Aedui to send him speedily all their cavalry and ten thousand infantry to garrison and protect his convoys of provisions. [Caesar] 52 BC: Caesar divides his army into two parts: Labienus is given four legions for the country of the Senones and Parisii, while Caesar leads six into the country of the Arverni toward Gergovia along the banks of the Allier. [Caesar] 52 BC: Vercingetorix breaks down all the bridges over the Allier and begins to march on the other bank. [Caesar]

Caesar in Gaul, 52 BC: Vercingetorix's rising, from Cenabum to Gergovia: 52 BC: Caesar writes that he feared being hindered from passing the river during the greater part of the summer, as the Allier cannot generally be forded before the autumn. [Caesar] 52 BC: Caesar stops behind with two legions in a secret place, sends on the rest with the baggage, and rebuilds the bridge on the same piles, the lower part of which remained entire. [Caesar] 52 BC: Cassius Dio writes that Caesar, with the best troops, cut timber and built rafts and crossed the stream on them while the barbarians still watched those marching ahead, supposing Caesar was among them. [Cassius Dio]

Caesar in Gaul, 52 BC: Vercingetorix's rising, from Cenabum to Gergovia: 52 BC: Vercingetorix, on learning that Caesar has crossed, goes before him by forced marches so as not to be compelled to come to an action against his will. [Caesar] 52 BC: Caesar writes that in five days' march he reached Gergovia and, after a slight cavalry skirmish, despaired of taking it by storm, the city being built on a very high mountain, and determined to take no measures to besiege it before he should secure a supply of provisions. [Caesar]

Caesar in Gaul, 52 BC: Vercingetorix's rising, from Cenabum to Gergovia: 52 BC: Vercingetorix pitches his camp on the mountain near the town, places the forces of each state separately and at small intervals around himself, and occupies all the hills of that range as far as they commanded a view of the Roman encampment. [Caesar] 52 BC: Caesar writes that Vercingetorix did not allow almost any day to pass without testing in a cavalry action, the archers being intermixed, what spirit and valour there was in each of his own men. [Caesar]

Caesar in Gaul, 52 BC: Vercingetorix's rising, from Cenabum to Gergovia: 52 BC: Caesar writes of a hill opposite the town, which if his men could gain they seemed likely to exclude the enemy from a great share of their supply of water and from free foraging, but which was occupied with a weak garrison. [Caesar] 52 BC: Caesar sets out from the camp in the silence of night, dislodges the garrison before succour could come from the town, posts two legions there, and draws from the greater camp to the less a double trench twelve feet broad. [Caesar]

Caesar in Gaul, 52 BC: Vercingetorix's rising, from Cenabum to Gergovia: 52 BC: Cassius Dio writes that the Gauls' fort was on a strong hill and was protected by mighty walls. [Cassius Dio] 52 BC: Cassius Dio writes that the barbarians kept guard over the fort at Gergovia after seizing all the high ground around, so that they could safely remain in position and, if they charged down, would usually have the advantage. [Cassius Dio] 52 BC: Napoleon III writes that on the western side the mountain of Gergovia is attached by a narrow defile of 120 metres in width, called the Goules, to the heights of Risolles. [Napoleon III]

Caesar in Gaul, 52 BC: Vercingetorix's rising, from Cenabum to Gergovia: 52 BC: Napoleon III gives the plateau, 380 metres above the plain, as 1,500 metres in length by more than 500 metres in breadth. [Napoleon III] 52 BC: Wikipedia says the heights of Gergovia stand 360 metres above the plain they overlook, a plateau 1,500 metres long by 700 metres wide. [Wikipedia] 52 BC: Convictolitanis the Aeduan, to whom Caesar had adjudged the magistracy, being bribed by the Arverni, holds a conference with young men, the chief of whom were Litavicus and his brothers. [Caesar]

Caesar in Gaul, 52 BC: Vercingetorix's rising, from Cenabum to Gergovia: 52 BC: It is resolved that Litavicus should have the command of the ten thousand Aedui who were being sent to Caesar for the war, and have charge of them on their march. [Caesar] 52 BC: About thirty miles from Gergovia, Litavicus suddenly convenes the soldiers and, weeping, tells them that Eporedorix and Viridomarus have been slain by the Romans without even permission to plead their cause. [Caesar] 52 BC: Litavicus points to the Roman citizens who had accompanied them in reliance on his protection, seizes a great quantity of corn and provisions, cruelly tortures them and then puts them to death. [Caesar]

Caesar in Gaul, 52 BC: Vercingetorix's rising, from Cenabum to Gergovia: 52 BC: Cassius Dio writes that Litavicus set out as if to fulfill his mission but sent ahead horsemen to say that the Aedui companions in the Roman camp had been arrested by the Romans and put to death. [Cassius Dio] 52 BC: Eporedorix, on learning the design of Litavicus, lays the matter before Caesar almost at midnight. [Caesar] 52 BC: Caesar draws out four light-armed legions and all the cavalry without hesitation, with no time to contract the camp, and leaves Caius Fabius, his lieutenant, with two legions to guard the camp. [Caesar]

Caesar in Gaul, 52 BC: Vercingetorix's rising, from Cenabum to Gergovia: 52 BC: After advancing twenty-five miles Caesar comes in sight of the army of the Aedui, orders his soldiers to kill no one, and has Eporedorix and Viridomarus move among the cavalry to address their friends; the Aedui extend their hands in submission and lay down their arms. [Caesar] 52 BC: Cassius Dio writes that Caesar sent to the Aedui the Aedui he had and who were thought to have been slain, so that all might see them alive, and followed on with his cavalry. [Cassius Dio]

Caesar in Gaul, 52 BC: Vercingetorix's rising, from Cenabum to Gergovia: 52 BC: Horse sent by Fabius tell Caesar that the camp was attacked by a very powerful army, fresh men frequently relieving the wearied. [Caesar] 52 BC: Caesar reaches the camp before sunrise owing to the very great zeal of his soldiers. [Caesar] 52 BC: The Aedui, on the first announcements from Litavicus, plunder the property of the Roman citizens and either massacre them or drag them away to slavery. [Caesar]

Caesar in Gaul, 52 BC: Vercingetorix's rising, from Cenabum to Gergovia: 52 BC: The Aedui, contaminated by guilt and charmed by the gains from the plundered property, begin to form plans of war and stir up the other states by embassies, while Caesar answers their ambassadors with as much mildness as he can. Caesar in Gaul, 52 BC: Vercingetorix's rising, from Cenabum to Gergovia: 52 BC: Caesar notices that the hill in the possession of the enemy was stript of men, although on former days it could scarcely be seen on account of the numbers on it. [Caesar] 52 BC: At dawn Caesar orders a large quantity of baggage drawn out of the camp and muleteers with helmets, in the guise of horsemen, to ride round the hills. [Caesar]

Caesar in Gaul, 52 BC: Vercingetorix's rising, from Cenabum to Gergovia: 52 BC: Caesar sends one legion to the same hill and, after it had marched a little, stations it in the lower ground and conceals it in the woods; the suspicions of the Gauls increase and all their forces are marched to that place to defend it. [Caesar] 52 BC: Caesar particularly advises his lieutenants to restrain their men from advancing too far through desire of fighting or hope of plunder, saying that success depended on a surprise and not on a battle. [Caesar]

Caesar in Gaul, 52 BC: Vercingetorix's rising, from Cenabum to Gergovia: 52 BC: Almost in the middle of the hill the Gauls had built a wall six feet high, made of large stones, as a barrier to retard the advance of the Romans. [Caesar]

Caesar in Gaul, 52 BC: Vercingetorix's rising, from Cenabum to Gergovia: 52 BC: Caesar orders the signal sounded for a retreat; the tenth legion halts, but the soldiers of the other legions, not hearing the trumpet because there was a very large valley between them, are nevertheless kept back by the tribunes and lieutenants according to Caesar's orders. [Caesar]

Caesar in Gaul, 52 BC: Vercingetorix's rising, from Cenabum to Gergovia: 52 BC: Lucius Fabius, a centurion of the eighth legion, who had said that day that he was excited by the plunder of Avaricum, is raised up by three men of his company and scales the wall. [Caesar]

Caesar in Gaul, 52 BC: Vercingetorix's rising, from Cenabum to Gergovia: 52 BC: Caesar, alarmed for the safety of his troops, orders Titus Sextius to lead out his cohorts from the smaller camp and post them at the foot of the hill on the right wing of the enemy. Caesar in Gaul, 52 BC: Vercingetorix's rising, from Cenabum to Gergovia: 52 BC: Marcus Petreius, a centurion of the same legion, after attempting to hew down the gates, is overpowered by numbers and, despairing of his safety, having already received many wounds, speaks to the soldiers of his own company who followed him. Caesar in Gaul, 52 BC: Vercingetorix's rising, from Cenabum to Gergovia: 52 BC: Caesar writes that the tenth legion, posted in reserve on ground a little more level, checked the Gauls in their eager pursuit, supported by the cohorts of the thirteenth legion under Titus Sextius. Caesar in Gaul, 52 BC: Vercingetorix's rising, from Cenabum to Gergovia: 52 BC: Wikipedia says Caesar ordered a general retreat to lure Vercingetorix off the high ground, but the order was not heard by most of Caesar's force. [Caesar] 52 BC: Caesar tells the soldiers not to attribute to the valour of the enemy what the disadvantage of position had caused. [Caesar]

Caesar in Gaul, 52 BC: Vercingetorix's rising, from Cenabum to Gergovia: 52 BC: Vercingetorix will not descend to the level ground; after a slight and successful cavalry action Caesar leads his army back into the camp, and the next day, thinking he had done enough to lower the pride of the Gauls, moves his camp in the direction of the Aedui. [Caesar] 52 BC: The enemy not pursuing, on the third day Caesar repairs the bridge over the river Allier and leads over his whole army. [Caesar]

Caesar in Gaul, 52 BC: Vercingetorix's rising, from Cenabum to Gergovia: 52 BC: Cassius Dio writes that Caesar lost a number of his soldiers, saw that the enemy could not be captured, and that, with an uprising among the Aedui, all these considerations led him to raise the siege. Caesar in Gaul, 52 BC: Vercingetorix's rising, from Cenabum to Gergovia: 52 BC: Caesar, though he now saw the treachery of the Aedui in many things, lets Viridomarus and Eporedorix depart, lest he should appear to offer an insult or betray some suspicion of fear. Caesar in Gaul, 52 BC: Vercingetorix's rising, from Cenabum to Gergovia: 52 BC: Caesar writes that Eporedorix and Viridomarus, on reaching Noviodunum, put to the sword the garrison and the traders, divided the money and horses among themselves, had the hostages brought to Bibracte, and burnt the town. [Caesar] 52 BC: Cassius Dio writes that the Aedui burned down Noviodunum, because of its advantageous situation, to prevent the Romans from making it a base for war. [Cassius Dio] 52 BC: Caesar writes that the Loire had swollen to such a degree from the melting of the snows that it did not seem capable of being forded at all. [Caesar]

Caesar in Gaul, 52 BC: Vercingetorix's rising, from Cenabum to Gergovia: 52 BC: Caesar makes very long marches by day and night to the Loire, contrary to the expectation of all, finds by means of the cavalry a ford, and disperses his cavalry to break the force of the current. [Caesar]

Caesar in Gaul, 52 BC: Vercingetorix's rising, from Cenabum to Gergovia: 52 BC: Labienus at first attempts to raise vineae and fill up the marsh with hurdles and clay; finding it too difficult, he leaves his camp in silence at the third watch and reaches Melodunum. [Caesar] 52 BC: Labienus seizes about fifty ships and quickly joins them together, and obtains possession of Melodunum without a contest. [Caesar] 52 BC: Caesar writes that it was reported that he had departed from Gergovia, and that intelligence was brought of the revolt of the Aedui and a successful rising in Gaul. [Caesar]

Caesar in Gaul, 52 BC: Vercingetorix's rising, from Cenabum to Gergovia: 52 BC: Labienus thinks he must adopt a very different system and not provoke the enemy to an action, but bring his army back safe to Agendicum. [Caesar] 52 BC: Labienus assigns the ships brought from Melodunum to Roman knights, one to each, and orders them to fall down the river silently for four miles, at the end of the fourth watch, and there wait for him. [Caesar] 52 BC: The enemy's scouts, not expecting an attack because a great storm had suddenly arisen, are surprised, and the infantry and cavalry of Labienus are quickly transported across the river. [Caesar]

Caesar in Gaul, 52 BC: Vercingetorix's rising, from Cenabum to Gergovia: 52 BC: At the seventh legion's tribunes' order the legion faced about to the enemy's rear and attacked it; all were surrounded and slain, and Camulogenus met the same fate. [Caesar] 52 BC: Cassius Dio writes that Labienus occupied the island in the Sequana after conquering its defenders on the nearer bank and sending his troops across at many points at once, both down and up stream. [Cassius Dio]

Caesar in Gaul, 52 BC: Vercingetorix's rising, from Cenabum to Gergovia: 52 BC: The revolt of the Aedui being known, the war grows more dangerous; having got possession of the hostages whom Caesar had deposited with them, the Aedui terrify the hesitating by putting them to death. [Caesar] 52 BC: A council of all Gaul is summoned to Bibracte; the decision is left to the votes of the mass, and all to a man approve of Vercingetorix as their general. [Caesar]

Caesar in Gaul, 52 BC: Vercingetorix's rising, from Cenabum to Gergovia: 52 BC: The Remi, Lingones and Treviri were absent from the council at Bibracte, the Remi and Lingones because they attached themselves to the alliance of Rome, the Treviri because they were remote and hard pressed by the Germans. [Caesar] 52 BC: The Aedui are highly indignant at being deprived of the chief command and miss Caesar's indulgence, but after engaging in the war do not dare to pursue their own measures apart from the rest. [Caesar] 52 BC: Vercingetorix demands hostages from the remaining states and orders all the cavalry, fifteen thousand in number, to assemble quickly. [Caesar]

Caesar in Gaul, 52 BC: Vercingetorix's rising, from Cenabum to Gergovia: 52 BC: Vercingetorix says he will be content with the infantry he had before and would not tempt fortune nor come to a regular engagement, but with abundance of cavalry could prevent the Romans from obtaining forage or corn if the Gauls destroyed their own corn and set fire to their houses. [Caesar] 52 BC: Vercingetorix levies ten thousand infantry on the Aedui and Segusiani, who border on the Roman province, adds eight hundred horse, and sets over them the brother of Eporedorix with orders to wage war against the Allobroges. [Caesar]

Caesar in Gaul, 52 BC: Vercingetorix's rising, from Cenabum to Gergovia: 52 BC: Caesar writes that the only guards provided against these contingencies were twenty-two cohorts collected from the entire province by Lucius Caesar, the lieutenant. [Caesar] 52 BC: The Helvii, voluntarily engaging in battle with their neighbours, are defeated, and Caius Valerius Donotaurus, the son of Caburus, the principal man of the state, and several others are slain, and they are forced to retire within their towns and fortifications. [Caesar]

Caesar in Gaul, 52 BC: Vercingetorix's rising, from Cenabum to Gergovia: 52 BC: Caesar, perceiving the enemy superior in cavalry and that he could receive no aid from the province or Italy, sends across the Rhine into Germany to the states he had subdued and summons cavalry and light-armed infantry. [Caesar] 52 BC: The German horsemen being mounted on unserviceable horses, Caesar takes horses from the military tribunes and the rest, even from the Roman knights and veterans, and distributes them among the Germans. [Caesar] 52 BC: When Caesar was marching into the country of the Sequani through the confines of the Lingones, Vercingetorix encamped in three camps about ten miles from the Romans. [Caesar]

Caesar in Gaul, 52 BC: Vercingetorix's rising, from Cenabum to Gergovia: 52 BC: Vercingetorix tells the commanders of the cavalry that the time of victory was come, that the Romans were fleeing into the province and leaving Gaul, and that they should attack them on their march, when encumbered. [Caesar] 52 BC: The cavalry unanimously shout that they ought to bind themselves by a most sacred oath that he should not be received under a roof, nor have access to his children, parents or wife, who shall not twice have ridden through the enemy's army. [Caesar]

Caesar in Gaul, 52 BC: Vercingetorix's rising, from Cenabum to Gergovia: 52 BC: On the next day the Gallic cavalry were divided into three parts, and two of these made a demonstration on the Roman flanks while one in front began to obstruct the march. [Caesar] 52 BC: Caesar orders his cavalry also to form three divisions and charge the enemy; the main body halts and the baggage is received within the ranks of the legions. [Caesar]

Caesar in Gaul, 52 BC: Vercingetorix's rising, from Cenabum to Gergovia: 52 BC: If the Romans seemed hard pressed in any quarter, Caesar usually ordered the troops to advance and the army to wheel round in that quarter, which retarded the enemy in the pursuit and encouraged his men by the hope of support. [Caesar] 52 BC: The Germans on the right wing gain the top of the hill, dislodge the enemy from their position and pursue them as far as the river at which Vercingetorix with the infantry was stationed; the rest, fearing to be surrounded, betake themselves to flight, and a slaughter ensues in every direction. [Caesar]

Caesar in Gaul, 52 BC: Vercingetorix's rising, from Cenabum to Gergovia: 52 BC: Three of the noblest of the Aedui are taken and brought to Caesar: Cotus, the commander of the cavalry, Cavarillus, and Eporedorix. [Caesar] 52 BC: Cassius Dio writes that Vercingetorix, filled with contempt for Caesar because of his reverses, marched against the Allobroges, and intercepting Caesar among the Sequani, surrounded him. [Cassius Dio] 52 BC: Cassius Dio writes that Vercingetorix's defeat was due in part to the Germans who were acting as allies of the Romans. [Cassius Dio]

Caesar in Gaul, 52 BC: Vercingetorix's rising, from Cenabum to Gergovia: 52 BC: Plutarch writes that the enemy fell upon Caesar and surrounded him with many tens of thousands, so that he essayed to fight a decisive battle. [Plutarch] 52 BC: Plutarch writes that many tribes had revolted, but the head and front of the revolt were the Arverni and Carnuntini. [Plutarch] 52 BC: Plutarch writes that if Vercingetorix had risen a little later, when Caesar was involved in the civil war, Italy would have been a prey to terrors no less acute than those aroused by the Cimbri of old. [Plutarch]

Caesar in Gaul, 52 BC: Vercingetorix's rising, from Cenabum to Gergovia: 52 BC: Plutarch writes that by the vigour and speed of his passage in so severe a winter Caesar showed the barbarians that an unconquered and invincible army was coming against them. [Plutarch] 52 BC: Plutarch writes that the nation of the Aedui also entered the war against Caesar, having up to this time called themselves brethren of the Romans, and by joining the rebels caused great dejection in Caesar's army. [Plutarch] 52 BC: Cassius Dio writes that the Arverni revolted and killed all the Romans they found in their cities and their country. [Cassius Dio]

Caesar in Gaul, 52 BC: Vercingetorix's rising, from Cenabum to Gergovia: 52 BC: Cassius Dio writes that Caesar made no attempt to help the Bituriges, since not all his soldiers were at hand as yet, but by invading the Arvernian country drew the enemy home again, whereupon he retired in good season, not deeming himself yet a match for them. [Cassius Dio] 52 BC: Cassius Dio writes that the invaders, going back to the Bituriges, captured Avaricum and held out in it for a long time, the wall being hard to approach, bordered on one side by almost trackless swamps and on the other by a river with a swift current. [Cassius Dio]

Caesar in Gaul, 52 BC: Vercingetorix's rising, from Cenabum to Gergovia: 52 BC: Napoleon III writes that Caesar established his camp near the Auzon, and that Vercingetorix had arranged the contingents of each country separately at small intervals on the southern slopes of the mountain of Gergovia. [Napoleon III]

The Siege of Alesia (52 BC – 1862-1865). The edge that decided it: Roman siege engineering — lines of works facing the town and facing outward let a smaller army hold a besieged town and a relief army at once.

What the sources say about the edge at The Siege of Alesia: "Caesar, caught between so large hostile forces and besieged there, was compelled to build two walls for his protection, one looking towards the city, and the other towards those who had come up to relieve it; he felt that if the two forces should unite his cause was wholly lost" [Plutarch] "he orders him, if he should be unable to withstand them, to draw off the cohorts and make a sally; but not to do this except through necessity. He himself goes to the rest, and exhorts them not to succumb to the toil" [Caesar]

What the sources say about the edge at The Siege of Alesia: "having enclosed an area of fourteen miles, he constructed, against an external enemy, fortifications of the same kind in every respect" [Caesar] "This line of circumvallation, of fourteen miles in circuit (twenty-one kilometres), had been formed on the most favourable ground" [Napoleon III]

Who's who in The Siege of Alesia: Julius Caesar — commander of the besieging Roman army; Vercingetorix — elected supreme commander of the Gallic confederation; besieged, then surrendered, at Alesia; Vergasillaunus (Vercassivellaunus) — Vercingetorix's cousin, joint commander of the relief army, led the final assault on the Mont Rea camp and was taken alive; Commius — Atrebatian chief, one of the four commanders entrusted with the relief army's supreme command; Titus Labienus — Caesar's lieutenant, sent with reserves to hold the threatened Mont Rea camp in the final battle.

Who's who in The Siege of Alesia: Critognatus — Arvernian noble inside Alesia, sprung from its noblest family and of great influence, who addressed the besieged as their food ran out; Napoleon III — emperor of the French; funded the 1862-1865 excavations that found the Roman works at Alesia.

The Siege of Alesia: 52 BC: Vercingetorix raises the Arverni in revolt; news of the Roman massacre at Genabum spreads across Gaul within a day. [Caesar] 52 BC: Vercingetorix, son of Celtillus, is chosen to lead the Gallic revolt after being driven out of Gergovia by his own uncle. [Caesar] 52 BC: Cassius Dio records the opening of the revolt: the Arverni under Vercingetorix kill every Roman in their territory. [Cassius Dio] 52 BC: Vercingetorix adopts a scorched-earth strategy, burning more than twenty Biturigan towns to deny Caesar supply, sparing only Avaricum. [Caesar]

The Siege of Alesia: 52 BC: Avaricum falls to Caesar; of roughly forty thousand inside, only about eight hundred reach Vercingetorix's camp alive. [Caesar] 52 BC: Caesar's assault on Gergovia fails with heavy loss; he publicly blames his soldiers' rashness rather than the enemy's valour. [Caesar] 52 BC: A council of all Gaul at Bibracte names Vercingetorix supreme commander of the confederation by unanimous vote; the Aedui resent losing the command. [Caesar] 52 BC: The Aedui, outvoted for the supreme command, remain openly resentful even as they stay in the coalition. [Caesar]

The Siege of Alesia: 52 BC: Caesar's German cavalry breaks Vercingetorix's horsemen at the Battle of the Vingeanne, forcing the Gauls back toward Alesia. [Caesar] September 52 BC: Vercingetorix withdraws into Alesia; Caesar follows and camps before the town, beginning the siege. [Caesar, Cassius Dio] September 52 BC: Cassius Dio confirms the shift from pursuit to blockade: Caesar shuts up the surviving Gauls inside Alesia. [Cassius Dio] September 52 BC: Napoleon III's excavation narrative dates the decision: Caesar resolves to invest the whole hill-town rather than storm it. [Napoleon III]

The Siege of Alesia: September 52 BC: The Roman line of investment facing the town runs eleven thousand paces, carried by camps and twenty-three redoubts on the surrounding heights. [Napoleon III] September 52 BC: Caesar then builds a second line, facing outward, fourteen miles in circuit, to meet the relief army he expects Gaul to send. [Napoleon III] September 52 BC: Caesar orders thirty days' forage and corn stockpiled so the Roman works need not be abandoned for want of supply. [Caesar]

The Siege of Alesia: 52 BC: Gaul's council levies a fixed quota of men by state rather than calling out the whole nation, reasoning it could not supply or command an unlimited host. [Caesar] 52 BC: The relief army assembles roughly eight thousand cavalry and about two hundred and forty thousand infantry under four joint commanders, including Commius and Vercingetorix's cousin Vergasillaunus. [Caesar] September 52 BC: With corn exhausted and no word of relief, the besieged debate surrender or a breakout; Critognatus proposes eating the old and useless rather than yield, as the Cimbri once did. [Caesar]

The Siege of Alesia: September 52 BC: The Mandubii, who had sheltered the Gallic army, are expelled from Alesia with their wives and children and begged the Romans, in vain, to take them as slaves. [Caesar] September 52 BC: Cassius Dio records that Vercingetorix had already tried the same expedient — thrusting out the women, children and useless mouths — and that both besiegers and besieged refused to take them back, so they died between the lines. [Cassius Dio]

The Siege of Alesia: September 52 BC: The relief army under Commius and the other Gallic leaders reaches Alesia and camps on the plain, in sight of the besieged, who celebrate at the sight of help. [Caesar] September 52 BC: A cavalry battle is fought in the plain between the lines; German horsemen in Roman pay break the Gallic cavalry and rout its archers. [Caesar] September 52 BC: The Gauls mount a night assault on the plain fortifications with hurdles, scaling ladders and hooks, signalling the besieged inside to rise at the same time. [Caesar]

The Siege of Alesia: September 52 BC: Sixty thousand picked Gauls under Vercassivellaunus are sent to storm the weak camp on Mont Rea, on the outward-facing line, while the rest assail the plain works. [Napoleon III] September 52 BC: Caesar commits his last reserves on both fronts at once, sending Labienus to the Mont Rea camp and riding himself to the plain to steady the line. [Caesar] September 52 BC: Caesar leads cavalry around the outer line to strike the Gallic relief force from the rear; the relief army breaks, Sedulius is killed, and Vergasillaunus is taken alive. [Caesar]

The Siege of Alesia: September 52 BC: Plutarch stresses that the final battle outside was fought and won without the besieged, or even the Romans guarding the town-facing wall, knowing it was happening. [Plutarch] September 52 BC: The besieging Romans only learn of their own victory outside when they hear the wailing of the Gauls inside Alesia, who have just seen the defeated relief army's gold-adorned shields and bloodied armour carried into the Roman camp. [Plutarch] September 52 BC: Vercingetorix offers his council the choice of killing him to appease Caesar or surrendering him alive; ambassadors are sent to negotiate. [Caesar]

The Siege of Alesia: September 52 BC: Caesar seats himself before his camp; the Gallic chieftains surrender Vercingetorix and lay down their arms, ending the siege. [Caesar] September 52 BC: Plutarch records the surrender scene differently: Vercingetorix rides out in his finest armour, circles Caesar, dismounts, strips his armour, and sits silently at Caesar's feet until taken into custody. [Plutarch] September 52 BC: Cassius Dio says Vercingetorix came to Caesar unannounced hoping their old friendship would win him pardon, and fell to his knees in supplication; Caesar was unmoved. [Cassius Dio]

The Siege of Alesia: 52 BC: Caesar distributes the surrendered Gallic captives, one to each soldier, as plunder, sparing the Aedui and Arverni to win over their states. [Caesar] 52 BC: Vercingetorix is kept in bonds and, after being displayed in Caesar's triumph years later, is put to death. [Cassius Dio] 52 BC: News of the victory reaches Rome; the senate decrees twenty days of public thanksgiving on Caesar's despatches. [Caesar, Napoleon III] 1862-1865: Commandant Stoffel's excavations for Napoleon III's history recover physical traces of the Roman works at Alesia, including five of the iron-hooked stakes (stimuli) Caesar describes planting in the ground between the lines. [Napoleon III]

Caesar in Gaul, 51–50 BC: Uxellodunum and the end of the war (52 BC – 51 BC). The edge that decided it: A hill town held out until its water was cut: archers on the stream, then a mine driven to the spring

What the sources say about the edge at Caesar in Gaul, 51–50 BC: Uxellodunum and the end of the war: "Caesar, perceiving the difficulty, disposed archers and slingers, and in some places, opposite to the easiest descents, placed engines, and attempted to hinder the townsmen from getting water at the river" [Caesar] "A mound sixty feet high was raised; on it was erected a turret of ten stories, not with the intention that it should be on a level with the wall (for that could not be effected by any works), but to rise above the top of the spring" [Caesar]

What the sources say about the edge at Caesar in Gaul, 51–50 BC: Uxellodunum and the end of the war: "At last the veins of the spring were cut across by our mines, and turned from their course. By this their constant spring was suddenly dried up, which reduced them to such despair" [Caesar] "Gaius Caesar, in one of his Gallic campaigns, deprived the city of the Cadurci⁠a of water, although it was surrounded by a river and abounded in springs; for he diverted the springs by subterranean channels, while his archers shut off all access to the river." [Frontinus]

What the sources say about the edge at Caesar in Gaul, 51–50 BC: Uxellodunum and the end of the war: "This gallery has been opened over an extent of forty metres. It was dug in a solid mass of tufa nearly ten metres thick" [Napoleon III]

Who's who in Caesar in Gaul, 51–50 BC: Uxellodunum and the end of the war: Julius Caesar — proconsul in command of Gaul; leaves the war and turns toward Rome; Titus Labienus — Caesar's lieutenant; sent against the Treviri, later governor of Cisalpine Gaul; Commius — Atrebatian chief; with the Bellovaci in 51 BC, then submits on condition he never meet a Roman; Napoleon III — emperor of the French; his history places Uxellodunum at the Puy-d'Issolu; Correus — Bellovacian leader killed in the ambush of 51 BC.

Who's who in Caesar in Gaul, 51–50 BC: Uxellodunum and the end of the war: Lucterius — Cadurcian who with Drapes seized Uxellodunum; Drapes — Senonian who with Lucterius held Uxellodunum; Gaius Caninius Rebilus — Caesar's lieutenant who began the siege of Uxellodunum; Gaius Fabius — Caesar's lieutenant sent with twenty-five cohorts who joined the siege; Gaius Trebonius — Caesar's lieutenant wintering at Genabum, called up to the Bellovacian campaign.

Who's who in Caesar in Gaul, 51–50 BC: Uxellodunum and the end of the war: Marcus Antonius — Caesar's quaestor, left in charge of his quarters; Dumnacus — general of the Andes defeated near the Loire; Epasnactus — Arvernian who handed Lucterius to Caesar; Guturvatus — Carnute whom Caesar had put to death; Ambiorix — Eburonian chief whose country Caesar laid waste.

Who's who in Caesar in Gaul, 51–50 BC: Uxellodunum and the end of the war: Caius Volusenus — Roman officer; sent to have Comius killed, later wounded by him; Pompey — consul and ruler of Spain; Caesar's rival at Rome; Gaius Curio — tribune of the people who took up Caesar's cause; Gaius Marcellus — consul of 50 BC, hostile to Caesar; Marcus Marcellus — consul of 51 BC who moved against Caesar's command.

Who's who in Caesar in Gaul, 51–50 BC: Uxellodunum and the end of the war: Aulus Hirtius — Caesar's officer, to whom Book VIII of the Gallic War is ascribed; Vercingetorix — the Arvernian chief who led the Gallic revolt of 52 BC; named in the introduction and chapter 2 as the leader the war had turned on.

Caesar in Gaul, 51–50 BC: Uxellodunum and the end of the war: 52 BC: Hirtius writes that, with Gaul entirely reduced and Caesar wishing to rest his soldiers in winter quarters after the former summer's incessant war, news reached Caesar that several states were renewing their hostile intentions and forming combinations. [Caesar] 52 BC: Hirtius gives the Gauls' reasoning: if several states made war in different places at the same time, the Roman army would have neither aid, nor time, nor forces to prosecute them all. [Caesar]

Caesar in Gaul, 51–50 BC: Uxellodunum and the end of the war: 52 BC: Caesar leaves Marcus Antonius, his quaestor, in charge of his quarters and sets out from Bibracte with a guard of horse the day before the kalends of January. [Caesar] 51 BC: Hirtius writes that Caesar's sudden arrival found an unprovided and dispersed people: his horse surprised them cultivating the fields before they had time to fly to their towns. [Caesar]

Caesar in Gaul, 51–50 BC: Uxellodunum and the end of the war: 51 BC: Hirtius writes that, as Caesar's activity obliged the wavering to accept offers of peace, the Bituriges, seeing that through his clemency an avenue was open to his friendship and that the neighbouring states had given hostages and been received under his protection without punishment, did the same. [Caesar] 51 BC: Caesar promises his soldiers two hundred sestertii each, and every centurion two thousand, to be given instead of plunder. [Caesar] 51 BC: Caesar, unwilling to expose his soldiers to the violent storms of that season, quarters his army at Genabum, a town of the Carnutes. [Caesar]

Caesar in Gaul, 51–50 BC: Uxellodunum and the end of the war: 51 BC: Frequent embassies from the Remi inform Caesar that the Bellovaci, led by Correus of the Bellovaci and Comius the Atrebatian, are raising an army; Hirtius says the Bellovaci exceed all the Gauls and Belgae in military prowess. [Caesar] 51 BC: Asked by Caesar where the main body of the Bellovaci was posted and what was their design, they answer that the Bellovaci had resolved to give him battle if he came with only three legions, and if he brought a stronger force to remain in the position they had chosen and by ambuscade prevent the Romans from getting forage. [Caesar]

Caesar in Gaul, 51–50 BC: Uxellodunum and the end of the war: 51 BC: Hirtius writes that Caesar had three veteran legions of distinguished valour, the seventh, eighth and ninth, and that the eleventh consisted of chosen youth who had served eight campaigns. [Caesar] 51 BC: Hirtius writes that Caesar marched with the seventh, eighth and ninth legions before all the baggage and the eleventh bringing up the rear, so that the enemy could not see more of his army than they were willing to encounter. [Caesar] 51 BC: Caesar encamps opposite the Bellovaci with a valley between them and orders a rampart twelve feet high and two trenches, each fifteen feet broad. [Caesar]

Caesar in Gaul, 51–50 BC: Uxellodunum and the end of the war: 51 BC: Hirtius says Caesar's works meant that, when forage was needed from afar, his camp could be held by a very small force. [Caesar] 51 BC: Comius returns with some cavalry from the Germans; Hirtius says the Germans were only 500, yet the barbarians were elated by their arrival. [Caesar] 51 BC: Finding the Bellovacian camp well secured by a morass and impossible to assault without a dangerous engagement or to enclose without more men, Caesar writes to Trebonius to send with all despatch for the thirteenth legion, then to come to him by forced marches with the three legions. [Caesar]

Caesar in Gaul, 51–50 BC: Uxellodunum and the end of the war: 51 BC: The Remi, to whom that day's duty had been allotted, despising the weakness of the enemy's cavalry, pursue them too eagerly, are surrounded on every side by the foot and return in disorder with the loss of Vertiscus, governor of their state and general of their horse. [Caesar] 51 BC: In one of these contests the Germans whom Caesar had brought over the Rhine cross the marsh, kill the few who resist and pursue the rest, so terrifying the enemy that they flee and do not stop till they have retired into their camp. [Caesar]

Caesar in Gaul, 51–50 BC: Uxellodunum and the end of the war: 51 BC: The Bellovaci, learning that Trebonius is approaching and fearing a siege like that of Alesia, send off by night those disabled by age or infirmity, with their baggage. [Caesar] 51 BC: Caesar lays a bridge over the marsh and leads his army across to the hill beyond. [Caesar] 51 BC: The Bellovaci hand forward the bundles of straw and sticks on which they sat, pile them in front of their line and at the close of day set them all on fire at once; the blaze screens their forces from the Romans and they flee. [Caesar]

Caesar in Gaul, 51–50 BC: Uxellodunum and the end of the war: 51 BC: Caesar learns from a prisoner that Correus has chosen six thousand foot and a thousand horse to lie in ambush where the Romans will come for forage. [Caesar] 51 BC: Forewarned, Caesar draws out more legions than usual and sends his cavalry forward as usual to protect the foragers, with a guard of light infantry intermixed. [Caesar] 51 BC: The ambushers, defeated and put to the rout and having lost the greater part of their men, flee in consternation wherever chance carries them. [Caesar]

Caesar in Gaul, 51–50 BC: Uxellodunum and the end of the war: 51 BC: Correus, unconquered by calamity, will not quit the field and take refuge in the woods or accept the Romans' offers of quarter, but fights courageously, wounding several, and provokes the Romans. [Caesar] 51 BC: The Bellovaci, learning that Correus was slain and their horse and most valiant foot cut off, unanimously resolve to send ambassadors and hostages to Caesar; Comius the Atrebatian flees to the Germans. [Caesar]

Caesar in Gaul, 51–50 BC: Uxellodunum and the end of the war: 51 BC: Caesar tells the Bellovacian ambassadors that he knew the guilt of a crime was easily transferred to the dead, but that no one person could, by the feeble support of the multitude, raise a war and carry it on without the consent of the nobles. [Caesar] 52 BC: Hirtius writes that the year before, while Caesar was holding the assizes in Hither Gaul, Labienus, having found Comius tampering with the states and raising a conspiracy against Caesar, sent Volusenus Quadratus with orders to have Comius put to death under pretence of a conference. [Caesar]

Caesar in Gaul, 51–50 BC: Uxellodunum and the end of the war: 51 BC: Hirtius writes that Caesar's legions and auxiliaries, sent through every part of Ambiorix's dominions, wasted the whole country by sword, fire and rapine and killed or took prodigious numbers. [Caesar] 51 BC: Caninius is informed that Duracius is shut up by several thousand men under Dumnacus, general of the Andes, and that Limonum is besieged; not daring to face the enemy with his weak legions, he encamps in a strong position. [Caesar]

Caesar in Gaul, 51–50 BC: Uxellodunum and the end of the war: 51 BC: When the Roman legions come in sight, the barbarian horse are astonished and the foot terrified and they flee in disorder; Hirtius says the Roman horse kept up the slaughter and killed above twelve thousand men in arms, or who threw away their arms through fear, and took their whole train of baggage. [Caesar]

Caesar in Gaul, 51–50 BC: Uxellodunum and the end of the war: 51 BC: Hirtius writes that Drapes, a Senonian, who had collected men of desperate fortunes, invited the slaves to liberty and called in the exiles, was marching to the province with five thousand men, all he could collect after the defeat, and that Luterius, a Cadurcian, had formed a junction with him. [Caesar] 51 BC: Luterius, with his own and Drapes' troops, seizes Uxellodunum, a town strongly fortified by its natural situation and once in vassalage to him, and prevails on the inhabitants to join him. [Caesar]

Caesar in Gaul, 51–50 BC: Uxellodunum and the end of the war: 51 BC: Caninius, finding all parts of the town secured by very craggy rocks, divides his forces into three parts and pitches three camps on very high ground, meaning to draw lines round the town by degrees. [Caesar] 51 BC: The townsmen, terrified by the recollection of the distress at Alesia, dread similar consequences from a siege, and Luterius, who had experienced that fatal event, cautions them to make provision of corn. [Caesar] 51 BC: Drapes and Luterius leave two thousand men in the garrison and march out of the town with the rest, by general consent, to bring in corn. [Caesar]

Caesar in Gaul, 51–50 BC: Uxellodunum and the end of the war: 51 BC: Caninius, on the report of the scouts, attacks the convoy at break of day with the ready-armed cohorts from the nearest turrets; his men fall with great fury on the escort and let not a single man be taken alive, and Luterius escapes with a few followers. [Caesar] 51 BC: Caninius learns from prisoners that part of the forces is encamped with Drapes, not more than ten miles off. [Caesar] 51 BC: Caninius's cohorts attack Drapes's force on every side, kill or capture them all, take great booty, and take Drapes himself prisoner. [Caesar]

Caesar in Gaul, 51–50 BC: Uxellodunum and the end of the war: 51 BC: The next day Caius Fabius comes with his forces to join him (Caninius) and takes upon himself the siege of one side. [Caesar] 51 BC: Hirtius writes that when Caesar came to the Carnutes he demanded that Guturvatus, promoter of the treason and instigator of the rebellion, be delivered up; Guturvatus was brought to the camp, and Caesar, forced by the soldiers' clamours contrary to his natural humanity, had him whipped to death and beheaded. [Caesar]

Caesar in Gaul, 51–50 BC: Uxellodunum and the end of the war: 51 BC: Hirtius gives Caesar's reason for severity: informed by Caninius's letters of the townsmen's persistence, he thought their obstinacy deserved severe punishment, lest Gaul conclude that she lacked perseverance rather than strength to oppose the Romans. [Caesar] 51 BC: Caesar knew that all the Gauls understood his command was to continue but one summer longer. [Caesar] 51 BC: Caesar arrives at Uxellodunum, contrary to general expectation, finds the town surrounded by the works, and, informed by deserters that the townsmen have abundance of corn, endeavours to prevent their getting water. [Caesar]

Caesar in Gaul, 51–50 BC: Uxellodunum and the end of the war: 51 BC: The river could not be turned from its course: it ran so low at the foot of the mountain that no drains could be sunk deep enough. [Caesar] 51 BC: Caesar places archers and slingers, and engines opposite the easiest descents, to stop the townsmen getting water at the river, which obliged them to go all to one place for water. [Caesar] 51 BC: Hirtius writes that close under the walls of the town a copious spring gushed out, on the part which for the space of nearly three hundred feet was not surrounded by the river. [Caesar]

Caesar in Gaul, 51–50 BC: Uxellodunum and the end of the war: 51 BC: Hirtius writes that, while everyone else wished the besieged could be cut off from the spring, Caesar alone saw that it could be done, though not without great danger. [Caesar] 51 BC: The Romans raise a mound sixty feet high with a turret of ten stories on it, not to match the wall but to rise above the top of the spring. [Caesar] 51 BC: Hirtius says that once Caesar's engines played from the turret on the paths to the fountain, not only the cattle but a great number of men died of thirst. [Caesar]

Caesar in Gaul, 51–50 BC: Uxellodunum and the end of the war: 51 BC: The Romans work mines and move crates and vineae to the source of the fountain, the one work they could do without danger or suspicion. [Caesar] 51 BC: The townsmen fill barrels with tallow, pitch and dried wood, set them alight and roll them down on the Roman works. [Caesar] 51 BC: Caesar orders his cohorts up the mountain on all sides to raise a shout as if assailing the walls; the besieged call their troops back to the walls and the Romans gain time to extinguish the works that had caught fire. [Caesar]

Caesar in Gaul, 51–50 BC: Uxellodunum and the end of the war: 51 BC: The veins of the spring are cut across by the Roman mines and turned from their course; the constant spring is suddenly dried up. [Caesar] 51 BC: The besieged, believing the drying of the spring the will of the gods and not the art of man, submit from necessity. [Caesar] 51 BC: Hirtius writes that Caesar, to deter others, cut off the hands of those who had borne arms against him and spared their lives so that the punishment would be conspicuous. [Caesar]

Caesar in Gaul, 51–50 BC: Uxellodunum and the end of the war: 51 BC: Hirtius writes that Caesar was convinced his lenity was known to all men and that he would not be thought to act from natural cruelty. [Caesar] 51 BC: Hirtius writes that Drapes, taken by Caninius, abstained from food for several days and perished, and that Luterius, fallen into the hands of Epasnactus, an Arvernian friend of the Roman people, was delivered a prisoner to Caesar. [Caesar] 51 BC: Labienus, in a cavalry action among the Treviri, takes their chiefs alive, among them Surus the Aeduan, the only Aeduan still in arms. [Caesar]

Caesar in Gaul, 51–50 BC: Uxellodunum and the end of the war: 51 BC: Caesar, reflecting that he had never gone in person to Aquitania, sets out for it with two legions; all its states send ambassadors and hostages. [Caesar] 51 BC: Caesar posts four legions in the country of the Belgae under Marcus Antonius, Caius Trebonius, Publius Vatinius and Quintus Tullius, two among the Aedui, two among the Turoni near the confines of the Carnutes, and the other two in the territories of the Lemovices, a small distance from the Arverni, so that no part of Gaul might be without an army. [Caesar]

Caesar in Gaul, 51–50 BC: Uxellodunum and the end of the war: 51 BC: Comius, clapping spurs to his horse, rides up to Volusenus and pierces him in the thigh with his lance. [Caesar] 51 BC: Comius, either having gratified his resentment or having lost the greatest part of his followers, sends to Antonius, offers hostages and obedience, and asks only that he never be made to go into the presence of any Roman; Antonius accepts his hostages. [Caesar] 50 BC: Hirtius states that the year of the consuls Lucius Paulus and Caius Marcellus produced no remarkable occurrences in Gaul. [Caesar]

Caesar in Gaul, 51–50 BC: Uxellodunum and the end of the war: 50 BC: Hirtius writes that Caesar kept Gaul, exhausted by so many unsuccessful battles, in obedience by treating the states with respect, giving presents to leading men, imposing no new burdens and lightening the terms of subjection. [Caesar] 50 BC: Caesar thinks himself in honour bound to visit the free towns and colonies, to thank them for their service to Antonius at the election and to recommend to them his own suit for the consulate the ensuing year; Hirtius says his adversaries boasted that Lucius Lentulus and Caius Marcellus had been appointed consuls, who would strip Caesar of all honour and dignity. [Caesar]

Caesar in Gaul, 51–50 BC: Uxellodunum and the end of the war: 50 BC: Hirtius writes that Caesar made Titus Labienus governor of Cisalpine Gaul so that he might be the more inclined to support him in his suit for the consulate. [Caesar] 50 BC: Hirtius writes that Curio, a tribune, proposed to the senate that Pompey and Caesar should both resign their commands and disband their armies and called on the senate to divide, but the consuls and Pompey's friends interposed to prevent it and broke up the meeting. [Caesar]

Caesar in Gaul, 51–50 BC: Uxellodunum and the end of the war: 50 BC: Hirtius says the senate decreed that Pompey and Caesar should each send a legion to the Parthian war, but both were evidently drawn from Caesar alone; Caesar sent back to Pompey the legion he had been given and ordered his own fifteenth to be delivered up. [Caesar] 50 BC: Hirtius ends: though it was evident to every one that war was designed against Caesar, he resolved to submit to anything while hope remained of settling the dispute equitably, rather than have recourse to arms. [Caesar]

Caesar in Gaul, 51–50 BC: Uxellodunum and the end of the war: 58–50 BC: Frontinus writes that Caesar, in one of his Gallic campaigns, deprived a city, though surrounded by a river and abounding in springs, of water: he diverted the springs by subterranean channels while his archers shut off all access to the river. [Frontinus] 50 BC: Dio writes that these wars came to an end in the consulship of Lucius Paulus and Gaius Marcellus, and that it was now time for Caesar, in view of the subjugation of the Gauls and the period for which his command had been assigned him, to leave Gaul and return to Rome. [Cassius Dio]

Caesar in Gaul, 51–50 BC: Uxellodunum and the end of the war: 50 BC: Dio writes that Caesar, afraid that if deprived of his soldiers he would fall into the power of Pompey or his other enemies, did not dismiss them. [Cassius Dio] 51 BC: Dio writes that Marcellus directed all his efforts at the downfall of Caesar, among other measures proposing that a successor be sent out before the appointed time. [Cassius Dio] 50 BC: Dio writes that Caesar made preparations to stay in office in spite of them (his enemies), collecting additional soldiers, gathering money and providing arms. [Cassius Dio]

Caesar in Gaul, 51–50 BC: Uxellodunum and the end of the war: 50 BC: Dio writes that Marcellus, when Curio was acquitted by the majority, went to Pompey in the suburbs and, without the formality of a vote, entrusted him with the protection of the city and two legions of citizens. [Cassius Dio] 50 BC: Dio writes that nominally both Pompey and Caesar contributed, but that in reality Caesar alone sent the two (legions). [Cassius Dio] 50 BC: Dio writes that the consuls' and Pompey's moves only displayed their enmity and gave Caesar a plausible excuse for retaining the legions; Curio, on finishing his term, at once set out to join Caesar. [Cassius Dio]

Caesar in Gaul, 51–50 BC: Uxellodunum and the end of the war: 50 BC: Dio writes that Caesar, by means of garrisons, punishments (the fetched scan prints 'punts'), levies of money and assessments of tribute, humbled some of the Gauls and tamed others. [Cassius Dio] 50 BC: Napoleon III writes that, after Gaul was subdued, Caesar was destined to find only auxiliaries there, and that his policy had contributed as much as his arms to this result. [Napoleon III] 1865: Napoleon III describes the Puy-d'Issolu as a lofty mountain near the right bank of the Dordogne, between Vayrac and Martel. [Napoleon III]

Caesar in Gaul, 51–50 BC: Uxellodunum and the end of the war: 1865: Napoleon III writes that the excavations proved that it (the spring he calls A) is produced by the waters which run in the Roman gallery, that the gallery has been opened over an extent of forty metres, and that it was dug in a solid mass of tufa nearly ten metres thick. [Napoleon III] 1865: Napoleon III reckons the distance from the spring to the Tourmente at about 300 metres, about 200 Roman paces, and holds that the Latin word pedum must be replaced by passuum. [Napoleon III]

Caesar in Gaul, 51–50 BC: Uxellodunum and the end of the war: 1865: Napoleon III writes that the digs on the slope of Loulie turned up Gaulish pottery and amphorae and remains of arms like those in the fosses of Alesia, a further confirmation of the identity of the Puy d'Issolu with Uxellodunum. [Napoleon III] 51 BC: Napoleon III writes that Caesar, seeing the place obstinately defended and abundantly provisioned, could not reduce it by force or famine and so conceived the idea of depriving the besieged of water, carrying a subterranean gallery to the veins of the spring that alone supplied their wants. [Napoleon III]

Caesar in Gaul, 51–50 BC: Uxellodunum and the end of the war: 51 BC: Napoleon III calls the cutting off of the hands an unpardonable act of cruelty, even though it might have appeared necessary. [Napoleon III] 51 BC: Napoleon III writes that of all the chiefs who fought for Gaul's independence only Commius and Ambiorix survived, and that, banished far from their country, they died unknown. [Napoleon III] 51 BC: Wikipedia says Fabius arrived with 25 cohorts, roughly two and a half legions, and that these reinforcements put the Roman forces at four and a half legions. [Wikipedia]

Caesar in Gaul, 51–50 BC: Uxellodunum and the end of the war: 51 BC: Hirtius gives Caninius two legions and Fabius twenty-five cohorts (his own figures, separate from Wikipedia's four and a half legions). [Caesar]

The Siege of Syracuse (216 or 215 BC – no year stated by any fetched source (Plutarch dates it only to "Marcellus's fourth consulship"; corrected 2026-10-19, finish stage, from the writing stage's flagged but unfixed "211 BC")). The edge that decided it: Archimedes' engines held off Rome's combined land-and-sea assault on Syracuse, so Marcellus's council resolved to blockade rather than storm; the city fell only later, by a night escalade during a festival of Diana/Artemis, and its inner citadel Achradina by treachery.

What the sources say about the edge at The Siege of Syracuse: "while as long as he remained there, they did not venture even to think of making the attempt, at least by any method which made it possible for Archimedes to oppose them" [Polybius] "At last Appius retired into the camp, and summoning the Tribunes to a council of war, decided to try every possible means of taking Syracuse except a storm" [Polybius]

What the sources say about the edge at The Siege of Syracuse: "Wherefore, a council being held, it was resolved, since every attempt was frustrated, to abstain from assaulting the place, and keeping up a blockade, only to cut off the provisions of the enemy by sea and land" [Livy] "For most of the engines on the walls had been devised by Archimedes, and the Romans thought that they were fighting against gods and not men" [Plutarch]

Who's who in The Siege of Syracuse: Archimedes — Syracusan mathematician and inventor, friend of Hiero II, whose engines defended the walls by land and sea and who was killed in the final sack; Marcus Claudius Marcellus — Roman consul and proconsul who commanded the naval assault, then the blockade, took the city by escalade, wept over its fate, and was later tried and acquitted over his treatment of it; Appius Claudius Pulcher — Roman propraetor/praetor who commanded the land assault and shared the blockade command with Marcellus; Hieronymus — young tyrant of Syracuse, grandson of Hiero II, whose alliance with Hannibal provoked the war with Rome; assassinated at Leontini after thirteen months; Hippocrates — Syracusan by descent but raised at Carthage; seized power with his brother Epicydes and led Syracuse's war effort against Rome; died of pestilence with the Carthaginian relief army.

Who's who in The Siege of Syracuse: Epicydes — brother of Hippocrates; co-general of Syracuse through the siege; per Livy, left Achradina to the mercenary commanders and fled to Bomilcar, then Agrigentum, before it fell -- did not hold it to the end (corrected 2026-10-19, chapter 4 writer/auditor); Hiero II — Syracuse's king for 54 years and Rome's ally, whose patronage funded Archimedes' siege engines before his death touched off the crisis; Bomilcar — Carthaginian admiral who twice tried and failed to break the Roman blockade by sea; Himilco — Carthaginian general who landed a relief army in Sicily; died with nearly all of it in the pestilence of 212 BC.

The Siege of Syracuse: 216 or 215 BC: Hiero II dies; his grandson Hieronymus succeeds him, upending Syracuse's relations with Rome. [Livy] 216 BC: An alliance is formed between Hannibal and Hieronymus, the tyrant of Syracuse. [Livy] 215 BC: Hieronymus is assassinated at Leontini only thirteen months into his reign. [Polybius] 215 BC: Epicydes and Hippocrates become Syracuse's leading generals and for a time feign willingness to make peace with Rome, sending legates to Marcellus. [Polybius] 214 BC: Hippocrates and Epicydes force their way into Syracuse, put most of the generals to death, and induce the mob, afraid of being betrayed to Rome, to elect them sole generals. [Polybius]

The Siege of Syracuse: 214 BC: Marcellus storms and takes Leontini, punishing deserters but sparing the townspeople. [Plutarch] 214 BC: Rome decrees the province of Sicily to Marcus Marcellus. [Livy] 214 BC: The Romans attack Syracuse at once by land at Hexapylus and by sea at Achradina. [Polybius] 214 BC: The Romans' plan does not take into account the abilities of Archimedes. [Polybius] 214 BC: Archimedes' catapults, built to suit every range, harass the Roman ships even while they are still far from the walls. [Livy, Polybius]

The Siege of Syracuse: 214 BC: Iron hooks worked by a counterweight seize some of the Roman ships, draw them up, and plunge them to the bottom. [Plutarch] 214 BC: Marcellus's great siege-engine 'the Harp,' mounted on a raft of lashed ships, is smashed by stones from the walls before it reaches them. [Plutarch] 214 BC: Reduced to despair, Marcellus brings up his ships under cover of night. [Plutarch, Polybius] 214 BC: The attempt to storm Syracuse from the sea is abandoned outright. [Polybius] 214 BC: Appius Claudius's land assault fails as well, and a council of war rules out any further attempt by storm. [Polybius]

The Siege of Syracuse: 214 BC: A Roman council of war resolves to abandon assaulting the city altogether and to blockade it instead, cutting off its supplies by land and sea. [Livy] 214-213 BC: For eight months of siege the Romans never again venture an assault on the walls. [Polybius] 214 BC: Appius and Marcellus divide their forces: Appius keeps two-thirds to maintain the blockade while Marcellus takes a third to campaign against other Sicilian cities. [Polybius] 213 BC: During the blockade Marcellus takes Megara, one of Sicily's oldest Greek cities, and storms Hippocrates' camp at Acrillae, killing more than eight thousand of his men. [Plutarch]

The Siege of Syracuse: 213 BC: A Carthaginian relief fleet of fifty-five warships under Bomilcar reaches Syracuse's Great Harbour. [Livy] 213 BC: Marcellus sees that the city cannot be taken by force, nor by famine while it is supplied without interruption. [Livy] 212 BC: The Carthaginians outside the city, with no place to retire to, perish to a man together with their generals Hippocrates and Himilco. [Livy] 212 BC: A deserter brings word that the Syracusans are keeping a three-day festival of Diana, celebrated the more freely with wine because other things are short. [Livy, Polybius]

The Siege of Syracuse: 212 BC: About a thousand armed men march in silence to the spot in a slender column and mount the wall without noise or confusion. [Livy] 212 BC: The rest of the force, with more ladders, mounts the wall on a signal given from the Hexapylos. [Livy] 212 BC: The Romans force open a postern gate near the Hexapylus and admit Marcellus and the rest of the army into the city. [Polybius] 212 BC: Marcellus bursts into tears, thinking how the city will be changed when his soldiers sack it. [Plutarch]

The Siege of Syracuse: 212 BC: The rest of the city is taken after a short time by treachery; the soldiers insist on plundering it, all but the royal treasury, which is confiscated to the state. [Plutarch] 212 BC: A Roman soldier, not recognizing him, kills Archimedes while he is absorbed in a geometric figure drawn in the dust; Marcellus is grieved at the news. [Livy, Plutarch] 212 BC: The royal treasury is secured for the Roman state while the rest of the city is given over to plunder by the soldiers. [Livy]

The Siege of Syracuse: 212 BC: Marcellus carries off most of Syracuse's famous artworks to be displayed in his triumph and to adorn Rome. [Plutarch] no year stated by any fetched source (Plutarch dates it only to "Marcellus's fourth consulship"; corrected 2026-10-19, finish stage, from the writing stage's flagged but unfixed "211 BC"): Syracusan envoys travel to Rome and complain to the Senate of Marcellus's harsh treatment of their city. [Plutarch]

The Siege of Syracuse: no year stated by any fetched source (Plutarch dates it only to "Marcellus's fourth consulship"; corrected 2026-10-19, finish stage, from the writing stage's flagged but unfixed "211 BC"): Marcellus restores the Syracusans their freedom, their laws and what remains of their property, and the Senate confirms his acts. [Plutarch]

The Siege of Xiangyang (1236 – 1279). The edge that decided it: Counterweight trebuchets (hui-hui pao, the "Muslim trebuchet"), built for the Mongols by engineers brought from the west, broke a siege that Song Xiangyang and Fancheng had held for five years; the Chinese, Persian, and Venetian sources agree foreign engineers decided it but disagree about who those engineers were.

What the sources say about the edge at The Siege of Xiangyang: "We thus see that three different notices of the siege of Siang-yang, Chinese, Persian, and Venetian, all concur as to the employment of foreign engineers from the West" [Marco Polo] "Fan-ch’eng could not hold out against such a barrage and fell several days after the weapons were employed" [De Re Militari]

What the sources say about the edge at The Siege of Xiangyang: "these new trebuchets were much more accurate than the old ones, and were the only artillery capable of reaching the walls of Xiangyang" [Wikipedia]

Who's who in The Siege of Xiangyang: Kublai Khan — Great Khan who ordered the siege and sent for the foreign engineers; Aju (A-chu) — Mongol commander who began the blockade of Xiangyang and Fancheng in 1268; Liu Zheng — Song defector who advised the Mongols to blockade and starve the cities; Lu Wenhuan — Song commander of Xiangyang who led breakout attempts and ultimately surrendered the city; Fan Wenhu — Song commander, Lu Wenhuan's father-in-law, who led a failed relief attempt in October 1270.

Who's who in The Siege of Xiangyang: Jia Sidao — Song chief councillor blamed by some sources for suppressing word of the siege's true danger; Bayan — Mongol general given overall command against the Song after the fall of Xiangyang; took the Song capital in 1276; Isma'il (Ismail) — Engineer the Chinese and De Re Militari accounts credit with building the counterweight trebuchets; Ala al-Din (Ala-ud-Din) — Engineer paired with Isma'il in the Chinese-derived accounts of the trebuchets; Alihaiya — Uighur general who, in the Chinese annals as Yule reports them, urged Kublai to send west for engineers.

Who's who in The Siege of Xiangyang: Nicolo Polo, Maffeo Polo, and Marco Polo — In Marco Polo's own account, the three Venetians whose advice and foreign craftsmen built the mangonels that took Saianfu; Abaqa, Ilkhan of Persia — Sent the foreign engineers to China at Kublai's request, per the Chinese-derived and Persian accounts.

The Siege of Xiangyang: 1236: Xiangyang surrenders to the Mongol army without resistance in 1236. [Wikipedia] 1257: The twin cities of Xiangyang and Fancheng, with walls almost five kilometres around and 200,000 people, withstand a Mongol assault in 1257. [Wikipedia] 1267: Kublai Khan orders Aju and the Song defector Liu Zheng to attack Xiangyang and Fancheng. [Wikipedia] 1268: Aju and Liu Zheng arrive and blockade the city with a ring of forts. [De Re Militari, Wikipedia] 1268: The Mongols under A-chu (Aju) and Liu Zheng surround Xiangyang with an unknown number of troops. [De Re Militari]

The Siege of Xiangyang: August 1269: In the siege's first naval battle, the Song general Hsia Kuei attacks Lu-men shan with 3,000 junks and is defeated; fifty of his junks are captured. [De Re Militari] March 1270: Xiangyang's commander Lu Wen-huan led a 10,000-strong breakout attempt against the Mongol siege lines. [De Re Militari] October 1270: A Song relief attempt under Fan Wen-hu tried to break through the Mongol blockade and failed, losing 2,000 men and thirty boats. [De Re Militari] August 1271: A second Song relief attempt failed, with the loss of 2,000 soldiers. [De Re Militari]

The Siege of Xiangyang: September 1272: Two Song commanders break through the Mongol lines with 3,000 men; one of them, Chang Shun, dies. [De Re Militari] 1272: Abaqa sends two renowned engineers, Isma'il of Hilla and Ala al-Din of Mosul, who build the first counterweight trebuchets in China, the hui-hui pao. [De Re Militari, Wikipedia] 1271: In the Chinese account, the Uighur general Alihaiya urges the emperor to send to the West for engineers who can build machines casting stones of 150 lbs. [Marco Polo]

The Siege of Xiangyang: late 1272: The Chinese annals, as Yule reports them, say the engineers reached the camp before Siang-yang and set up their engines in the latter part of 1272. [Marco Polo] early 1273: The Mongols open the final siege with Fancheng in early 1273. [Wikipedia] early 1273: Fancheng fell within days of the new trebuchets being brought to bear, after years of holding out. [De Re Militari, Wikipedia] 1273: The hui-hui pao are moved across the river and placed at the southeast corner of Xiangyang. [De Re Militari]

The Siege of Xiangyang: 14 March 1273: Xiangyang's commander Lu Wenhuan surrendered the city and was made governor of both cities under Yuan rule as part of the terms. [Wikipedia] 1273: In Marco Polo's account, the fall of Saianfu came about through the exertions of his father Niccolo, his uncle Maffeo and himself: his claim, which the other accounts contradict (edgeEvidence). [Marco Polo] 1275: With Xiangyang fallen, the Song government tried and failed to negotiate a truce with the Mongols. [Wikipedia] 1276: Bayan rides at the head of his whole staff with the standard of the general-in-chief before him. [Encyclopaedia Britannica, Marco Polo]

The Siege of Xiangyang: 1276: The Song capital surrenders in 1276, and Bayan rides into the city. [Encyclopaedia Britannica] 1279: In 1279 the last Song resistance is extinguished; the minister who inspired it ends the struggle by jumping into the sea with his young lord. [Encyclopaedia Britannica]

The Spanish Armada (1588-05 – 1588-07-28). The edge that decided it: English ships built to sail and fire at range, fireships at Calais, then weather and supply, against a fleet built to grapple and board.

What the sources say about the edge at The Spanish Armada: "the enemy's object will be to engage at a distance, on account of the advantage which they have from their artillery and the offensive fire- works with which they will be provided ; and on the other hand, the object on our side should be to close and grapple and engage hand to hand." [Navy Records Society] "My fortune was to make choice to charge their starboard wing without shooting of any ordnance until we came within six score" [Navy Records Society]

What the sources say about the edge at The Spanish Armada: "Instead, the Spanish gunners fired once and then transferred to their main task, which was to board enemy ships, as had been the practice in naval warfare at the time." [Wikipedia] "the Lord Admiral, the 28th of July, 1588, about midnight, caused eight ships to be fired and let drive amongst the Spanish fleet" [Navy Records Society]

Who's who in The Spanish Armada: Charles Howard, Lord Admiral — English commander-in-chief of the fleet; Francis Drake — English vice-admiral; John Hawkins — English rear-admiral and Treasurer of the Navy; Lord Henry Seymour — English commander of the Narrow Seas squadron; William Wynter — English squadron commander, wrote the Gravelines account used here.

Who's who in The Spanish Armada: Alonso Perez de Guzman, 7th Duke of Medina Sidonia — Spanish commander of the Armada; Alexander Farnese, Duke of Parma — Commander of the invasion army waiting in Flanders; Francisco de Cuellar — Spanish captain, eyewitness of the wreck of his ships on the Irish coast; Juan Martinez de Recalde — Spanish admiral commanding the rear-guard against the first English attack off Plymouth; Don Hugo de Moncada — Captain-general of the Armada's galleasses, son of the Viceroy of Valencia, killed defending the grounded San Lorenzo at Calais.

Who's who in The Spanish Armada: Arceo — Medina Sidonia's secretary, sent to carry word to Parma at Dunkirk while the fleet lay off Calais; Richard Tomson — Lieutenant of the Margaret and John of London, who boarded the grounded galleass San Lorenzo and left an eyewitness account; John Knox Laughton — The historian who edited the English state papers on the Armada, published in 1894; Colin Martin and Geoffrey Parker — Modern historians whose research into the ships that returned gives the campaign's losses as a whole; Elizabeth I — Queen of England, the invasion's intended target, who reviewed her land forces at Tilbury.

Who's who in The Spanish Armada: Philip II — King of Spain, who ordered the Armada's sailing and set its commander's instructions; James Anthony Froude — A nineteenth-century historian whose narrative of the Calais fireships and the voyage home the book draws on; José Luis Casado Soto — A modern historian who traced the fate of each Armada ship individually; Sir Francis Walsingham — Elizabeth's secretary of state and spymaster, recipient of Howard's and Wynter's letters, who later had the San Juan de Sicilia destroyed at Tobermory; Don Pedro de Valdés — Spanish squadron commander whose ship Nuestra Señora del Rosario was fouled and lost in the Channel and taken by Drake.

Who's who in The Spanish Armada: Thomas Fenner — English commander who signed the council's resolution to break off the chase and wrote of the storm's damage to the Armada; Martin de Aranda — Judge advocate of the Armada, who protected Cuéllar from execution and whose own ship nearly sank in the Irish storm; William FitzWilliam — English Lord Deputy of Ireland, who ordered Spanish survivors of the Irish wrecks killed; Monsieur de Gourdan — Governor of Calais, who warned Medina Sidonia of the dangerous currents and later claimed the grounded galleass for France; Henry Whyte — English captain who gave up his ship the Bark Talbot as a fireship and judged the attempt's effect afterward.

Who's who in The Spanish Armada: Álvaro de Bazán, Marquis of Santa Cruz — Spanish admiral first appointed to command the Armada, who died before it sailed; Martin de Bertendona — Commander of the Armada's Levant squadron, who offered to board the English flagship off Portland; Don Francisco de Toledo — Spanish colonel aboard the galleon San Felipe, who tried to grapple with the English at Gravelines; Robert Dudley, Earl of Leicester — The Queen's lieutenant-general against the invasion, who gathered the militia at West Tilbury; Don Christobal de Avila — Spanish captain of a victualler, condemned with Cuéllar for sailing ahead of the fleet and hanged.

Who's who in The Spanish Armada: André Marek y Villarino de Brugge — Modern biographer of Parma, cited for the time Parma's army needed to embark; Hugh Bicheno — Modern historian, cited for the English sailors who died of disease after the campaign; John Guy — Modern historian, cited for the English sailors who died of disease after the campaign; Cesáreo Fernández Duro — Spanish naval captain and historian who published the Spanish Armada papers in the 1880s; Henry Dwight Sedgwick — Translator of Cuéllar's letter into English.
Who's who in The Spanish Armada: Luis Gorrochategui Santos — Modern historian, cited in the afterword for the Armada never turning from a fight while the English kept their distance.

The Spanish Armada: 1588-05: By the middle of May the fleet is ready to sail from the Tagus. [Wikipedia] 1588-07-27: The Spanish fleet anchors east of Scales Cliffs, close together, not far from the shore. [Navy Records Society, Wikipedia] 1588-07-28: Howard sends eight fireships drifting into the anchored Spanish fleet at midnight. [Navy Records Society] 1588-07-28: The Spanish ships are forced to slip or cut their cables and set sail. [Navy Records Society]

The Spanish Armada: 1588-07-29: The galleass's commander is forced the next day to row ashore near the haven's mouth and town of Calais. The Spanish Armada: 1588-07-29: Spanish accounts, as Laughton reports them, estimate the English expenditure of shot at about three times their own. [Navy Records Society] 1588-08-08: At Gravelines the Spanish gunners fire once, then turn to their main task, boarding. [Navy Records Society] 1588-08-12: Howard calls off the chase off the Firth of Forth. [Navy Records Society, Wikipedia]

[Wikipedia] 1588-09: El Gran Grifón is wrecked on Fair Isle, putting around 260 soldiers and crew ashore there. [Wikipedia] 1588: After the campaign, disease kills English sailors who survived the fighting.
