The Spanish Armada: 1588-07-28: In Froude's account, Medina Sidonia, instead of sending launches to tow the fireships clear, signals the whole fleet to get under way at once. [James Anthony Froude]

The Battle of Hampton Roads (1861-04-20 – 1862-12-31). The edge that decided it: Two ironclads decided Hampton Roads: the Virginia's iron casemate and ram made the Union's wooden blockading fleet unable to resist her on 8 March 1862, and the Monitor's armor and revolving turret fought her to a standstill on 9 March, ending the battle in a draw that left the blockade intact.

What the sources say about the edge at The Battle of Hampton Roads: "clearly establishing the fact that wooden vessels can not contend successfully with ironclad ones; for never before was anything like it dreamed of by the greatest enthusiast in maritime warfare." [Navy Department] "the crash below the water was distinctly heard, and she commenced sinking, gallantly fighting her guns as long as they were above water." [Navy Department]

What the sources say about the edge at The Battle of Hampton Roads: "Gun after gun was fired by the Monitor , which was returned with whole broadsides from the rebels with no more effect, apparently, than so many pebblestones thrown by a child." [Navy Department] "The unusual federal vessel, however, soon won the respect of friend and foe alike, fighting the Confederate ironclad to a standstill in an exhausting four-hour duel." [Naval History and Heritage Command]

Who's who in The Battle of Hampton Roads: Franklin Buchanan — Flag-Officer commanding the Confederate James River Squadron and the Virginia on 8 March; severely wounded that afternoon; Catesby ap Roger Jones — Executive and ordnance officer of the Virginia; commanded her after Buchanan was wounded, including the fight with the Monitor on 9 March; John Taylor Wood — Lieutenant commanding a pivot gun on the Virginia on both days; wrote 'The First Fight of Iron-Clads' (Battles and Leaders, 1887); John L. Worden — Lieutenant commanding the Monitor; blinded in the pilothouse by a shell burst on 9 March; Samuel Dana Greene — Executive officer of the Monitor; took command when Worden was wounded and wrote the ship's official report.

Who's who in The Battle of Hampton Roads: Gershom J. Van Brunt — Captain of the frigate Minnesota, grounded through both days of the battle; his official report is the fullest Union eyewitness account of both ironclads; John Ericsson — Swedish-born engineer who designed and built the Monitor under contract to the Navy Department; John M. Brooke — Confederate naval officer who proposed and helped design the Virginia's conversion from the burned Merrimack; John L. Porter — Naval constructor who drew the working plans for rebuilding the Merrimack as the Virginia.

The Battle of Hampton Roads: 1861-04-20: The frigate Merrimack burns only to the waterline; her engines survive more or less intact. [Wikipedia] 1861-07-11: The new design for rebuilding the Merrimack as an ironclad is accepted, and work begins almost immediately. [Wikipedia] 1861-07-11: A written order directs that the changes to the Merrimac's form be made, and that she be built and equipped, with all practicable dispatch. [Century Co.] 1861: Jones is kept aboard the Virginia, but only as her executive officer. [Wikipedia] 1861-10-04: The Navy Department awards John Ericsson the contract to build the ironclad that becomes the Monitor. [Naval History and Heritage Command]

The Battle of Hampton Roads: 1862-01-30: The Monitor is launched; she is commissioned on 25 February 1862 with Lt. John L. Worden in command. [Naval History and Heritage Command] 1862-02-17: The rebuilt ironclad is commissioned CSS Virginia. [Wikipedia] 1862-03-06: The Monitor departs the New York Navy Yard under tow, bound for the Virginia capes. [Naval History and Heritage Command] 1862-03-08: The Virginia leaves the Norfolk Navy Yard at 11 a.m., escorted by the gunboats Beaufort and Raleigh, to attack the Union frigates Cumberland and Congress at Newport News. [Navy Department]

The Battle of Hampton Roads: 1862-03-08: With a crash heard below the water, the Cumberland begins to sink, fighting her guns as long as they are above water. [Navy Department] 1862-03-08: The Minnesota's captain tries to force her over the soft bottom and finds it impossible. [Navy Department] 1862-03-08: The Virginia drives the Congress ashore; she hauls down her colors and hoists the white flag, and fire with the white flag flying wounds Lieutenant Minor and some of the Virginia's men (the Virginia's account). [Navy Department] 1862-03-08: Flag-Officer Buchanan is wounded in the left thigh by a Minie ball that grazes the femoral artery. [Navy Department]

The Battle of Hampton Roads: 1862-03-08: The burning Congress's loaded guns discharge one by one as the fire reaches them, until her magazine explodes shortly after midnight. [Navy Department] 1862-03-08: The Monitor, which had arrived off Hampton Roads the previous evening, comes alongside the grounded Minnesota and reports for duty, raising the crew's hopes. [Navy Department] 1862-03-09: At daybreak the Virginia's officers, returning to finish the Minnesota, discover the Monitor lying between them and their target. [Century Co.]

The Battle of Hampton Roads: 1862-03-09: An observer describes the Monitor as an immense shingle floating on the water with a gigantic cheese box rising from its center: no sails, no wheels, no smokestack, no guns. [Naval History and Heritage Command] 1862-03-09: The Virginia keeps firing at the Minnesota, blows up a steamer alongside her, and engages the Monitor, sometimes at very close quarters. [Navy Department] 1862-03-09: A shell bursts against the Monitor's pilothouse, severely injuring Lieutenant Worden's eyes; he hands command to Lieutenant Greene. [Navy Department] 1862-03-09: Minnesota's captain, Van Brunt, watching the two ironclads trade fire, concludes wooden warships can no longer fight ironclad ones. [Navy Department]

The Battle of Hampton Roads: 1862-03-09: Van Brunt describes the Monitor's gunnery striking the Virginia's armor with no visible effect, like pebblestones thrown by a child. [Navy Department] 1862-03-09: Asked about his guns, a lieutenant aboard the Virginia replies that their powder is very precious, after two hours' incessant firing. [Century Co.] 1862-03-09: The Virginia's heavier draught of 22 feet, against the Monitor's 12, confines her to a narrow channel and lets the Monitor always keep her in range. [Century Co.] 1862-03-09: Two shots strike the Virginia's shield about half-way up, abreast of the after pivot, and force the side in bodily two or three inches. [Century Co.]

The Battle of Hampton Roads: 1862-03-09: The Monitor fights the Virginia to a standstill in an exhausting four-hour duel. [Naval History and Heritage Command] 1862-03-10: The New York Herald's dispatch headlines that the Monitor beat them off and disabled the Merrimac: 'SPLENDID SUCCESS OF THE MONITOR.' [The New York Herald] 1862-03-09: Stanton warns that the Merrimac will change the whole character of the war, destroy every naval vessel in turn, and lay all the cities on the seaboard under contribution. [Century Co.]

The Battle of Hampton Roads: 1862-03-10: Reporting to President Davis in Richmond, Lieutenant Wood says the Virginia has met her equal in the Monitor and another engagement's result would be very doubtful. [Century Co.] 1862: The London Times reckons that where Britain had one hundred and forty-nine first-class warships for immediate purposes, it now has two. [Century Co.] 1862: Britain and France, the era's preeminent naval powers, halt further construction of wooden-hulled warships in the battle's wake. [Wikipedia] 1862-04-11: The Virginia makes a brief appearance off Sewell's Point, but neither side forces a second engagement between the two vessels. [Naval History and Heritage Command]

The Battle of Hampton Roads: 1862-05-11: Too deep in draft to reach Richmond, the Virginia is set afire on 11 May and blows up soon after. [Naval History and Heritage Command] 1862-12-31: The Monitor founders in a storm off Cape Hatteras shortly after midnight on 31 December; four officers and twelve men go down with her. [Naval History and Heritage Command]

The Battle of Midway (1942-03-04 – 1942-06-04). The edge that decided it: Codebreakers at Station HYPO in Pearl Harbor read enough of the Japanese naval operational code (JN-25) to tell Admiral Nimitz, in advance, that the Japanese objective was Midway and roughly when the attack would come -- letting him position three carriers to ambush a Japanese force that still believed it had the advantage of surprise.

What the sources say about the edge at The Battle of Midway: "communications intelligence had given the United States a "priceless advantage" over the Japanese." [NSA Center for Cryptologic History] "Application of the new information to translations known to contain dates relevant to the forthcoming operation allowed Rochefort to predict that the Japanese attack on the Aleutians would occur on 3 June and on Midway on 4 June."
